subtitle: Whose: the genitive, and the little words that bring it
words.intro: Walk through a German town and read the doors. *Wegen Krankheit geschlossen. Wegen Umbau geschlossen.* The genitive lives on these signs, and in a very few people who insist on it.

grammar[0].fact: Roman ruins hold up German building sites all the time, from Cologne to Regensburg. When anything old turns up, work stops until an archaeologist has seen it. Some underground stations in Cologne have been built around what they found.

grammar[1].fact: A German *Bauamt* can take a very long time. Berlin’s new airport opened nine years late. Stuttgart’s railway project, begun in 2010, has taken far longer than planned. People from other cities bring this up with pleasure, even from a traffic jam of their own.

document.intro: A real road sign in Germany, all at once: a sign to say you can’t enter, a dead end, and a yellow arrow. The small white sign has the key phrase. *Anlieger* are the people who live on the street.
document.fact: You’ll see *Anlieger frei* everywhere: only people who live or have business on this street may drive in. A driver who says *ich bin Anlieger* at a building site may be believed, or not.
reading.intro: Frau Huber’s cousin Ernst runs a small shoe shop in a small town. He is proud of two things: forty years without a day off, and his German. Maya has stopped by, because of a sign in the window that she’s trying to read aloud.
reading.fact: A German bestseller is called *Der Dativ ist dem Genitiv sein Tod*: the dative is the death of the genitive. In speech, nearly everyone now says *wegen dem Regen*; in writing, *wegen des Regens* is still correct. So the book made its author, Bastian Sick, very rich.
